item.title: 🟠 The AI deregulation illusion: Why CIOs face more rules, not fewer
item.description:
Why this matters: Service impact is possible — verify vendor status before troubleshooting internally.

If you follow the headlines coming out of Washington, you might conclude that AI regulation is on its way out. The administration has made reducing regulatory barriers a priority, arguing that lighter oversight is essential to American innovation and competitiveness. But for CIOs responsible for deploying AI across large enterprises, the reality is exactly the opposite.

While Washington pushes for fewer restrictions, states are passing new AI legislation, international regulators are enforcing increasingly complex requirements, and lawmakers are turning their attention to how businesses actually use AI. Essentially, while AI may be getting deregulated at the federal level, it’s becoming more regulated in practice.

For organizations operating across state and national borders, this creates an increasingly difficult challenge. An AI application that meets requirements in one jurisdiction may trigger additional obligations in another. And as AI becomes embedded in more business-critical processes, the consequences of inadequate governance are growing.

At 09:24 on a quiet Tuesday, an AI agent spots suspicious privileged activity. It concludes the safest move is to turn off the identity service. So it does.

Everything works as designed. The agent has its own identity. Its credentials are scoped. The action lands in a log nobody can alter. The policy was clear enough: don’t interrupt production services without approval. The agent read the policy, weighed the threat and decided containment counted as approval.

By 09:30, the call centre can’t log in. Neither can the payments team.

Three good executives arrive in the same room with three different instincts. The CIO wants the service back. The CISO wants it kept down until someone proves the threat has gone. The CRO is doing quieter arithmetic, working out how long the firm can limp before it breaches a tolerance the board signed off last spring.

item.title: 🔵 Cloud repatriation is on the rise — but tricky questions remain
item.description:
Why this matters: Compliance/regulatory signal — determine applicability and required action.

Enterprises are moving to the cloud faster than they have in years. Nearly three-quarters (74%) of IT decision-makers say their organizations sped up cloud migration over the past 12 months, according to Foundry’s 2026 Cloud Computing Study.

Yet a growing number are also bringing some workloads back in-house. About two-thirds (66%) say their organizations have moved or plan to move workloads out of public cloud.

“Repatriation is one part of a wider rethink of where workloads belong,” says Mukesh Ranjan, vice president at Everest Group, a research and advisory firm.

AI workloads are part of the calculus. They’re leaving public cloud nearly as often as storage and databases, and just 13% of IT decision-makers plan to run AI primarily there, according to Foundry’s research. For CIOs, that means deciding workload by workload where each one belongs, with AI adding new factors to weigh, from GPU costs to where models run and where prompts are processed.

item.title: 🔵 The illusion of AI productivity in software development and what to measure instead
item.description:
Why this matters: Leadership context — useful for risk, budget, vendor, and strategic conversations.

Accenture reports that 82% of C-suite leaders are increasing AI investments, signaling continued confidence in the technology. But if you talk to tech leaders, the returns aren’t so clear-cut. AI can write code in seconds, but that’s only the first stage of software development. When AI-generated output introduces errors, misses internal requirements or requires extensive rework, the time saved upfront can quickly disappear.

A report from Bain & Co validates this — AI coding tools are helping developers complete roughly 21% more tasks, but time spent reviewing outputs rose 91%. As engineers generate more code, senior developers face growing review queues. AI can also produce lengthy specifications and documentation that take time to evaluate. This obscures the impact AI adoption is having on the software development lifecycle and, much of the time, simply creates more work.

item.title: 🔵 Mitigate memory price increases with components harvested from retiring devices
item.description:
Why this matters: Could affect sign-ins, MFA, or Conditional Access — watch for authentication issues.

The circular economy just picked up one of its strongest business cases yet, and it didn’t come from a sustainability mandate. It came from a memory shortage. An AI-induced memory shortage has pushed the price of new devices up, causing organizations to recalculate their repair-vs-replace threshold, and to look again at what a decommissioned device is still worth.

Rather than proceeding with typical 3 to 4-year refresh cycles, many IT and procurement teams have shifted to preservation mode, holding devices longer where they can and stretching the cycle. Another trend gaining ground: internal component harvesting. Instead of treating retiring or broken laptops as something to dispose of, forward-thinking organizations are treating them as sub-component mines. This means pulling the working memory and graphics cards out of a device too old to redeploy, and putting them into devices that can.

Procurement can buy memory at the new price, or pull it from a device it just decommissioned. The rest of this article covers the three main steps that make the second option work.

item.description:

Barely halfway through July and they’ve not only overshot their monthly budget but need an even larger allocation. This request, among many others, made us think twice about AI spend. The interest is there and often the innovation is, too. But what about the value? For decades, enterprise software development relied on an assumption that developers could experiment relatively safely because there were safeguards between their work and production. Development, staging and production had different rules, with human intermediaries making judgments about what was ready to move forward. item.title: 🔴 Why does old access outlive the job?
item.description:
Why this matters: Credential/phishing risk — reinforce MFA and watch for suspicious sign-ins.

Old access persists beyond its intended purpose and most organizations never monitor it. New access rights arrive within a day of a request. Old rights get revoked, if they get revoked at all, only upon prompting someone. Tools that assist employees in confirming, rotating and vaulting their service accounts have taught me again and again that removing access has to be as thoughtful as granting access. Security professionals can bridge this chasm with simple changes to their policies for role moves and access reviews.

This happens all the time. An employee moves from one team to another. The new manager approves the access needed for the new role within a day, and the person is productive by lunch. The access from the old role stays. After months, access review has one query only: “Do you still need it?” The reviewer sees the name next to the entitlement, but nothing on the dashboard shows whether it has been used since the move. It is hard to click no, because something might get broken. They have never been bothered to click yes. Thus, they click yes, and it’s fine by them.
